newsitem.title: UK: UK insurers fear tax rise from budget.
newsitem.headline: UK insurers fear tax rise from budget.

text.p: British insurers are worried that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke may target both the general insurance industry and long term savers as part of efforts to secure a headline-grabbing cut in income tax in next Tuesday's budget.

Fears of a hike in insurance premium tax (IPT), which applies to most forms of general insurance, proved unfounded last year, but with an election at most six months away, an increase this time is more likely, said insurance analysts.
In addition, the Association of British Insurers (ABI) is worried that the government may be considering a reduction in tax recovery for pensions, personal equity plans and charities.
"If I was a betting man, I'd probably bet that Clarke will go for some sort of increase (in IPT) this year," said insurance analyst John Marr at Charterhouse Tilney.
IPT was introduced by the current government in its November 1993 budget. The current rate is 2.5 percent, which will raise about 750 million pounds ($1.26 billion) in 1996 to 1997.

If the tax does go up, the industry consensus is for a rise to around six percent, raising about one billion pounds for the Treasury. Insurers would probably choose not to absorb any of this, passing it on to customers through higher prices.
The British insurance industry this week renewed a campaign attacking the tax. It has lobbied for the levy to be withdrawn, arguing the public was against an increase.

"It bears most strongly on the weakest and I think it will result in a reduction in premium income and losses being borne by those who don't have insurance and reinsurance," John Robins, Guardian Royal Exchange chief executive told Reuters.
"The tax is both oppressive and regressive," said the ABI's general director Mark Boleat. "We must ensure an IPT increase is swiftly removed from the Chancellor's possible hit list."

But despite a survey which the ABI said showed a six percent rise in IPT would cause many policyholders to review their insurance arrangements, industry analysts think such an increase would be unlikely to hit demand for insurance.

A cyclical slump in premium rates, made steeper than previous downturns by the advent of low cost direct selling over the telephone, means prices are much lower than they were two years ago and there is little evidence yet of a recovery.

But a bigger than expected increase in IPT to nearer ten percent, for example, could be more damaging. Insurers may opt to absorb some of that and share prices in the sector may sink if the stock market thinks this is a prelude to further rises.
The ABI is also concerned that the government might be considering a reduction of up to five percent in tax recovery for pensions, personal equity plans (PEPs) and charities.
"We are very concerned at minimising that effect," the ABI's deputy general director Tony Baker told Reuters.
One of Britain's biggest life assurers, Standard Life, said on Thursday the government should simplify the taxation system surrounding investments.

"The long term aim of the government must be to encourage individuals together with employers to make provision for their retirement and possible illness or incapacity," said Standard Life's marketing manager Andrew Black.
He also suggested Clarke should raise the limit for annual contributions to a general personal equity plan, which has not moved for seven years, by 3,000 pounds to 9,000 pounds. ($1=.5940 Pound)
